Q: What does .NET DateTime Ticks represent when Kind is Unspecified? A:

Perhaps you have confused the time zone and calendar? By default, dates are expressed in the Gregorian calendar, which follows the well-known calculation rule:

  • 1 day = 86400 seconds
  • 1 year has 365 or 366 days based on the year value

Observing the table below

Ticks Date and Time
0 0001-01-01 00:00:00.0000000
1 0001-01-01 00:00:00.0000001
86400 * 1E7 0001-01-02 00:00:00.0000000
365 * 86400 * 1E7 0002-01-01 00:00:00.0000000
621355968000000000 1970-01-01 00:00:00.0000000
639081143060012345 2026-03-03 05:58:26.0012345

It can be seen that without considering daylight saving time, you can calculate them without knowing the time zone. So Ticks represent the count of 100 nanoseconds that have passed since 0001-01-01, it's not related to Kind.

The Kind property only needs to be considered when comparing two DateTimes or converting a DateTime to another time zone.

Q: Using R to count instances of strings where the order of the letters isn't important A:

For each string, sort its characters, put them back together and count the frequencies with table.

fun <- function(x) {
  lapply(x, strsplit, "") |> 
    unlist(recursive = FALSE) |>
    lapply(sort) |> 
    sapply(paste, collapse = "") |>
    table(useNA = "ifany")
}

fun(offspring)
#> 
#> aabb aabB aaBB aAbb aAbB aABB AAbb AAbB AABB 
#>    1    2    1    2    4    2    1    2    1

Created on 2026-03-03 with reprex v2.1.1

You can output as a data.frame by piping the above to as.data.frame.

fun(offspring) |> as.data.frame()
#>   Var1 Freq
#> 1 aabb    1
#> 2 aabB    2
#> 3 aaBB    1
#> 4 aAbb    2
#> 5 aAbB    4
#> 6 aABB    2
#> 7 AAbb    1
#> 8 AAbB    2
#> 9 AABB    1

Q: Pi Pico Embedded Rust Always elf2uf2-r Always Produces Error: "Unrecognized ABI" A:

Quick guess: you need install libudev-dev

To isolate environmental issues, Docker is used to build the compilation environment.

I'm setting up a Docker environment to compile the pico program.

Create a directory: RaspberryPi_Pico_Rust

Directory Tree:

RaspberryPi_Pico_Rust
├── Dockerfile
├── docker-compose.yml
└── pico-buzzer <== All the same file contents as your code.
    ├── build.rs
    ├── Cargo.toml
    ├── memory.x
    └── src
        └── main.rs

Dockerfile

FROM rust:1.84-slim-bookworm

# Install the system dependencies required for compilation
# (e.g., elf2uf2-rs requires libudev).
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    pkg-config \
    libudev-dev \
    git \
    file \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install the Rust cross-compilation target platform (RP2040 uses Cortex-M0+).
RUN rustup target add thumbv6m-none-eabi

# Installation, burning, and auxiliary tools
RUN cargo install elf2uf2-rs flip-link

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

docker-compose.yml

version: '3.8'
services:
  pico-dev:
    build: .
    volumes:
      - ./pico-buzzer:/app
      - cargo-cache:/usr/local/cargo/registry
    tty: true
    stdin_open: true

volumes:
  cargo-cache:

Build

In RaspberryPi_Pico_Rust directory, run command:

docker-compose up -d

output:

Creating raspberrypi_pico_rust_pico-dev_1 ... done

Access the container's internal terminal

docker-compose exec pico-dev bash

output:

root@3f474836be2a:/app#

make sure current /app is mapping to your host pico-buzzer directory.

root@3f474836be2a:/app# ls -la
total 28
drwxrwxr-x 4 1000 1000 4096 Mar  3 06:17 .
drwxr-xr-x 1 root root 4096 Mar  3 06:24 ..
drwxrwxr-x 2 1000 1000 4096 Mar  3 06:01 .cargo
-rw-rw-r-- 1 1000 1000  634 Mar  3 06:01 Cargo.toml
-rw-rw-r-- 1 1000 1000  242 Mar  3 06:01 build.rs
-rw-rw-r-- 1 1000 1000  176 Mar  3 06:02 memory.x
drwxrwxr-x 2 1000 1000 4096 Mar  3 06:01 src

Now in the container.

Run Command:

cargo clean
cargo build --release

output:

...
   Compiling pio v0.2.1
   Compiling rp2040-hal v0.10.2
    Finished `release` profile [optimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 17.62s

elf2uf2-rs target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico-buzzer

output: Output nothing. Everything is fine. No error output.

use ls and file check output file.

  • ls -la target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico-buzzer.uf2
  • file target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico-buzzer.uf2

Output:

root@3f474836be2a:/app# ls -la target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico-buzzer.uf2
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 10240 Mar  3 06:28 target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico-buzzer.uf2

root@3f474836be2a:/app# file target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico-buzzer.uf2
target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico-buzzer.uf2: UF2 firmware image, family Raspberry Pi RP2040, address 0x10000000, 20 total blocks

you can see the message:

UF2 firmware image, family Raspberry Pi RP2040, address 0x10000000, 20 total blocks

In container:

exit

Then , In the Host:

close and exit docker container.

docker-compose down

Q: Why use 32-bit register when the data type is 64-bit? A:

The answer lies in Section 3.4.1.1 of the Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer’s Manual Volume 1 (Basic Architecture) which states:

When in 64-bit mode, operand size determines the number of valid bits in the destination general-purpose register:

  • 64-bit operands generate a 64-bit result in the destination general-purpose register.
  • 32-bit operands generate a 32-bit result, zero-extended to a 64-bit result in the destination general-purpose register.
  • 8-bit and 16-bit operands generate an 8-bit or 16-bit result. The upper 56 bits or 48 bits (respectively) of the destination general-purpose register are not modified by the operation. If the result of an 8-bit or 16-bit operation is intended for 64-bit address calculation, explicitly sign-extend the register to the full 64-bits.

See the second bullet.

You can gain some insight as to why this is so by reading: Why do x86-64 instructions on 32-bit registers zero the upper part of the full 64-bit register?
